events.title: WCEE Exhibition. The Art of Memory, Paintings by Felix Lembersky
events.summary: Felix Lembersky (1913-1970) was a painter, theater stage designer, teacher, and leader of artistic groups. He began his career within the Soviet Avant-Garde in Ukraine before studying realist painting in Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg). Throughout his life he worked across realist and modernist styles that fell outside of Soviet-mandated Socialist Realism. His Execution: Babyn Yar series (ca. 1944-52) is the earliest known artistic representation of Babyn Yar, a Holocaust massacre site in Kyiv. For political reasons, these paintings, along with his later nonconformist work, were barred from exhibition in the Soviet Union. Having witnessed two world wars, the 1917 revolution, and political terror, Lembersky reflected on these experiences with candor while imbuing his work with hope and optimism. He was drawn to vulnerable, neglected, and marginalized people: children, the elderly, ethnic minorities, and industrial workers subjected to harsh labor and dangerous conditions. Regardless of their circumstances, Lembersky portrayed his subjects with empathy, dignity, and admiration. “For my father, honesty and integrity meant more than anything else. Art was an expression of freedom, individuality, and personalized creativity, without which it ceased to be art.” — Galina Lembersky, daughter Exhibit curated by Yelena Lembersky, granddaughter of Felix Lembersky, and Geneviève Zubrzycki, WCEE Director. Works on loan from the private collection of Yelena Lembersky. Contact weisercenter@umich.edu to schedule a viewing. If there is anything we can do to make this event accessible to you, please contact us at weisercenter@umich.edu. Please be aware that advance notice is necessary as some accommodations may require more time for the university to arrange.

events.title: Faster and More Fun: American Home Cooking in the 1920s
events.summary: Visit the Hatcher Gallery Exhibit Room to see historical materials that illustrate women’s changing relationship with food, cooking, and technology during the heady decade of the 1920s, sandwiched between WWI and the Great Depression. This exhibit features materials from the Janice Bluestein Longone Culinary Archive, as well as select items from the Art, Architecture, and Engineering Special Collections and the Transportation History Collection. As America rang in a new decade in the 1920s, cookbook authors and appliance manufacturers stood ready to offer the newly emancipated and forward-thinking American woman a vision for her future, a vision that would be scientifically grounded, speedy enough to make time for leisure as well as housework, and guaranteed to bring fun to that most humdrum of chores: planning and preparing meals for a family three times a day, 365 days a year.

events.title: CSAS Lecture Series | What is the Private Life of Caste in India? The caste economies of India's success story
events.summary: Please note: This lecture will be held in person and virtually on Zoom. If you would like to attend via Zoom, registration is required. Once you've registered, joining information will be sent to your email. Register for the Zoom webinar at: https://myumi.ch/399y2 In this talk Thiranagama will draw from her book *The Monster in Your Path: The Private Life of Caste in India* on the situated histories of caste and enslavement in the South Indian state of Kerala, most often understood as India's success story. Thiranagama will discuss how new forms of caste disparities, as well as caste formations, have become sedimented not in the “public,” the center of most contemporary work, but rather in the new kinds of private spaces and private lives that arose after Kerala’s land reforms and communist transformation. Thiranagama suggests new ways to think about contemporary inequalities within historical economies of humiliation and subordination, as well discussing the dignity projects embarked upon by Kerala’s Dalit communities. Sharika Thiranagama is professor of anthropology at Stanford University. Her research explores violence, inequality, and intense political mobilization through a focus on intimacy, gender and generation. She has been the author of multiple works on Sri Lanka including *In My Mother’s House: Civil War in Sri Lanka* (University of Pennsylvania Press, 2011). Her most recent book *The Monster in Your Path* (University of California 2026) focuses on Dalit communities in Kerala, South India examining the gendered inheritance and life of enslavement, caste and work. If there is anything we can do to make this event accessible to you, please contact us. events.title: Biomedical Engineering (BME 500) Seminar Series
events.summary: At the Cell–Matrix Interface: Inflammatory Signaling and the Mechanobiology of Tendinopathy Abstract: Tendinopathy is a common and often persistent musculoskeletal disorder characterized by extracellular-matrix disorganization, altered tissue mechanics, and chronic inflammatory signaling. Yet the mechanisms linking changes in the extracellular matrix to sustained cellular dysfunction remain incompletely understood. This seminar will examine how nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) signaling contributes to tendon degeneration and repair, with emphasis on the reciprocal relationship between tendon cells and their extracellular matrix. Using biomechanical, cellular, and preclinical models, our work shows that dysregulated NF-κB activity can drive chronic tendon pathology and impair healing, while targeted modulation of this pathway may improve tendon-to-bone repair. I will also discuss emerging evidence that matrix composition and mechanics shape fibroblast inflammatory responses, metabolism, and mechanosensing. Together, these studies position the cell–matrix interface as a critical regulator of tendinopathy and a promising target for therapeutic development.. Bio: Adam C. Abraham, PhD, is an Assistant Professor of Orthopaedic Surgery at the University of Michigan. Trained in mechanical engineering, biomedical engineering, musculoskeletal biology, and immunology, Dr. Abraham studies how mechanical loading, extracellular-matrix properties, and inflammatory signaling interact to regulate connective-tissue health and disease. His laboratory focuses on tendon mechanobiology and pathophysiology, particularly the role of cell–extracellular matrix interactions in controlling fibroblast behavior and chronic inflammation. Dr. Abraham’s research has helped establish NF-κB signaling as a mechanistic driver and potential therapeutic target in tendinopathy and tendon-to-bone healing. His current National Institutes of Health-funded work examines how the extracellular matrix regulates inflammatory signaling in tendon. By integrating multiscale biomechanics, engineered tissue models, and preclinical disease models, his research seeks to identify mechanisms that can be translated into improved treatments for tendon injury and degeneration.

events.title: WCEE Exhibition. The Art of Memory, Paintings by Felix Lembersky
events.summary: Felix Lembersky (1913-1970) was a painter, theater stage designer, teacher, and leader of artistic groups. He began his career within the Soviet Avant-Garde in Ukraine before studying realist painting in Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg). Throughout his life he worked across realist and modernist styles that fell outside of Soviet-mandated Socialist Realism. His Execution: Babyn Yar series (ca. 1944-52) is the earliest known artistic representation of Babyn Yar, a Holocaust massacre site in Kyiv. For political reasons, these paintings, along with his later nonconformist work, were barred from exhibition in the Soviet Union. Having witnessed two world wars, the 1917 revolution, and political terror, Lembersky reflected on these experiences with candor while imbuing his work with hope and optimism. He was drawn to vulnerable, neglected, and marginalized people: children, the elderly, ethnic minorities, and industrial workers subjected to harsh labor and dangerous conditions. Regardless of their circumstances, Lembersky portrayed his subjects with empathy, dignity, and admiration. “For my father, honesty and integrity meant more than anything else. Art was an expression of freedom, individuality, and personalized creativity, without which it ceased to be art.” — Galina Lembersky, daughter Exhibit curated by Yelena Lembersky, granddaughter of Felix Lembersky, and Geneviève Zubrzycki, WCEE Director. Works on loan from the private collection of Yelena Lembersky. Contact weisercenter@umich.edu to schedule a viewing. events.title: Notion in Ionia: An International Symposium at the University of Michigan
events.summary: The cultural history of Ionia in western Türkiye resonates with many of the major concerns of contemporary Mediterranean archaeology: the transition from the Bronze Age to the Iron Age; different modes of human mobility, including migration and colonization; interaction between the Greek world and the Near East, especially in the Persian era; the evolution of the city, in particular the Greek polis in the Hellenistic period; Roman imperialism and its effects on subject peoples; and religious and economic change in late antiquity. Recent research in the region of the Hales River valley, dominated by the inland city of Colophon, the port town of Notion, and the rural sanctuary of Apollo at Claros, has shed new light on all these subjects. This two-day symposium at the Kelsey Museum of Archaeology examines the results of ongoing survey and excavation at Notion in the context of its larger regional and supra-regional environments. Free and open to the public, the event will also focus on intellectual collaboration between Turkish and American students and scholars. +Learn+ more about the symposium at https://myumi.ch/Pb5PV. +View+ the full program at https://myumi.ch/G75bP. If you have any questions or concerns regarding accessing this event, please visit our accessibility page at https://myumi.ch/zwPkd or contact the education office by calling (734) 647-4167. events.title: Voice & Piano Master Class with Cameron Stowe
events.summary: Pianist Cameron Stowe is a leading specialist in the study and performance of song recital repertoire, and he will lead a master class with SMTD voice and collaborative piano students in a variety of art songs. Free and open to the public; presented with generous support from the Sally Fleming Master Class Series. ABOUT THE GUEST ARTIST Dr. Stowe has appeared in concert venues and music festivals in the Far East, Europe, South America, and throughout the United States and Canada, playing with some of the most prominent singers of his generation, including Randall Scarlata, Denyce Graves, Reginald Mobley, Susan Graham, Danielle DeNiese, Faith Esham, Vinson Cole, Sari Gruber, Jesse Blumberg, and Oral Moses. Stowe serves as Chair of Collaborative Piano at New England Conservatory and Director of Collaborative Piano and Art Song Programming at Aspen Music Festival. Formerly a professor for fifteen years at The Juilliard School, he has given master classes to pianists and singers in the US and abroad, including residencies at Vancouver International Song Institute, Toronto Summer Music Festival, and National Taiwan Normal University. Recent educational projects include the creation of the innovative Song Lab at NEC and extensive work with musicologist Benjamin Binder, with whom he has designed song workshops and summer courses for performers, musicologists, theorists, and literary scholars. Together, they led the Scholarship in Song Performance summer festival at University of British Columbia for four years, assembling students and professionals, including Susan Youens, Jane Brown, Richard Kramer, Michael Musgrave, Graham Johnson, Thomas Allen, Ann Murray, and Margo Garrett, to encourage cross-disciplinary approaches in the study of song. In addition, Stowe served as keynote speaker and artist-teacher at the first Chinese National Conference on Collaborative Piano. Stowe holds a doctorate from The Juilliard School with a specialized focus in song and vocal chamber music, as well as degrees from Peabody Conservatory and Oberlin College Conservatory.

events.title: Food As Resistance
events.summary: Food as Resistance is an annual event during MLK week, hosted by Food Literacy for All and Michigan Dining. Doors open at 6:00 p.m. for mingling and small dishes prepared by the Michigan Dining chefs, who draw inspiration from their cultural backgrounds and understanding of food as a form of resistance. The program starts around 6:30, when keynote speaker Betti Wiggins will share her wisdom through a talk titled "From Food Insufficiency to Food Security: More Than a Consumer Relationship With Food." About Our Keynote: Betti Wiggins is a retired school food professional, educator, and food-systems advocate whose relationship with food began long before it became her profession. Raised on a farm in Augusta Township, Whittaker, Michigan, Wiggins grew up experiencing food as something a family participated in producing, not simply something it purchased. Growing food, preserving the harvest, and raising and processing animals for food were part of her childhood. Those experiences never left her. For Wiggins, the past is prologue: the lessons she learned on the farm would later shape her belief that children need a deeper connection to the food that sustains them. Her career took her through major school districts across the country, including serving as Director of School Food Service for Ann Arbor Public Schools from 1989 to 1992. In Detroit Public Schools, Wiggins began purchasing locally from farmers and food manufacturers, expanding children’s access to fresh fruits and vegetables, and developing school gardens as places of learning. Her willingness to challenge conventional thinking about school food earned her the nickname “Rebel Lunch Lady.” Her school gardens were grounded in a philosophy that connected directly to her own childhood experience: “Kids need to have more than a consumer relationship with food.” She wanted children to plant, grow, harvest, taste, ask questions, and understand that they, too, could be participants in the food system. Her work with children in school gardens became the subject of Miss Betti, What Is This? written by Laura Nargis and published by Sleeping Bear Press. In Houston Independent School District, Wiggins expanded that vision through Mykawa Farm, a 6.5-acre experiential learning farm for pre-K–12 students, where young people could experience food and agriculture firsthand. Her work also extended to food distribution during Pandemic for families, guided by another fundamental belief: “Hungry families send us hungry kids.” Feeding children at school was important, but she believed supporting children also meant working toward food-sufficient households. Now retired, Wiggins draws on a lifetime of experiences, from a Michigan farm to school gardens, local food purchasing, experiential learning, and family food distribution, in her current keynote on food insufficiency, food insecurity, and creating a more meaningful relationship between children, families, and the food system. Her story has come full circle. The childhood lessons of growing, preserving, and producing food became the foundation of a career dedicated to helping another generation understand that food is more than something we consume. It is something we are participating in.

events.title: Black Birth Joy
events.summary: Black Birth Joy by Tiana Lashae documents birth as a deeply personal story of connection, courage, tenderness, and joy. The photographs and stories in the exhibit challenge mainstream narratives that reduce Black birth to statistics and only amplify Black pregnant women's anxiety and hesitancy about navigating the maternal health care system. Instead, the exhibit offers evidence of joy, reminders of possibility, and a visual legacy for generations to come. Black Birth Joy was born from Lashae's belief that more positive birth stories of BIPOC families need to be seen and heard, and her photographs invite viewers to witness the people behind them: the mothers, babies, partners, families, and birthworkers. They create space for BIPOC families to see themselves represented with dignity and to witness the full range of birth experiences. Lashae's photographs also create a tangible record that can support conversations around quality of medical care, respectful treatment, and patient rights. The exhibit empowers women to prioritize and advocate for their birth experiences while also encouraging perinatal health professionals and birthworkers to center the humanity, dignity, and individual experiences of patients and families. The exhibit comprises over 30 photographs as well as stories of mothers whose births were documented by Lashae, a doula and birth/newborn photographer whose work has been published in Everyday Birth Magazine, an international publication. The physical exhibit is accompanied by a virtual component that encourages audiences to engage with each mother's birth story. The Lane Hall Exhibit Space is sponsored by the Institute for Research on Women and Gender (IRWG) and the Department of Women’s and Gender Studies (WGS) at the University of Michigan. events.title: IES Energy Seminar Series -  Hierarchy and Imperfect Competition in Power Markets afflicted by Uncertainty
events.summary: Abstract: Models for horizontal and hierarchical competition in power markets have been a source of significant interest over the last several decades. Yet less is known above computing equilibria in such settings particularly in the face of uncertainty. In this talk, we discuss flexible modeling paradigms for capturing Nash and Stackleberg equilibria in such settings. We briefly discuss computational methods for rigorous computation of equilibria in such settings. Time permitting, we pose some open questions in this setting. Biography: Uday V. Shanbhag is currently the Katta G. Murty Collegiate Professor and has been at the department of Industrial and Operations Engineering at the University of Michigan at Ann Arbor since Fall, 2024. From January 2017 to June 2024, he held the Gary and Sheila Chaired Professorsip in the department of Industrial and Manufacturing Engineering (IME) at the Pennsylvania State University, having been a tenured associate professor until 2016, since arriving in Fall 2012. Prior to being at Penn. State, from 2006–2012, he was first an assistant professor, and subsequently a tenured associate professor (for approx. 10 days), in the department of Industrial and Enterprise Systems engineering (ISE) at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign (UIUC). He serves on the editorial boards of the SIAM Journal of Optimization, the Mathematics of Operations Research, Computational Optimization and its Applications, and the Journal of Optimization Theory and Applications. Uday V. Shanbhag has a Ph.D. from Stanford University's department of Management Science and Engineering (2006), with a concentration in operations research and was associated with the Systems Optimization Laboratory when at Stanford. He also holds masters (1998) and undergraduate (1993) degrees from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), Cambridge (in Operations Research) and the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT), Bombay, respectively. For the most up to date information on the location, please check the related link the week of this event

events.title: WCEE Exhibition. The Art of Memory, Paintings by Felix Lembersky
events.summary: Felix Lembersky (1913-1970) was a painter, theater stage designer, teacher, and leader of artistic groups. He began his career within the Soviet Avant-Garde in Ukraine before studying realist painting in Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg). Throughout his life he worked across realist and modernist styles that fell outside of Soviet-mandated Socialist Realism. His Execution: Babyn Yar series (ca. 1944-52) is the earliest known artistic representation of Babyn Yar, a Holocaust massacre site in Kyiv. For political reasons, these paintings, along with his later nonconformist work, were barred from exhibition in the Soviet Union. Having witnessed two world wars, the 1917 revolution, and political terror, Lembersky reflected on these experiences with candor while imbuing his work with hope and optimism. He was drawn to vulnerable, neglected, and marginalized people: children, the elderly, ethnic minorities, and industrial workers subjected to harsh labor and dangerous conditions. Regardless of their circumstances, Lembersky portrayed his subjects with empathy, dignity, and admiration. “For my father, honesty and integrity meant more than anything else. Art was an expression of freedom, individuality, and personalized creativity, without which it ceased to be art.” — Galina Lembersky, daughter Exhibit curated by Yelena Lembersky, granddaughter of Felix Lembersky, and Geneviève Zubrzycki, WCEE Director. Works on loan from the private collection of Yelena Lembersky. Contact weisercenter@umich.edu to schedule a viewing. If there is anything we can do to make this event accessible to you, please contact us at weisercenter@umich.edu. Please be aware that advance notice is necessary as some accommodations may require more time for the university to arrange.

events.title: Harnessing Small Molecules in Primary and Secondary Metabolism: Insights from the Metalloenzymes Cytochrome P460 and DarE
events.summary: Metalloenzymescatalyze a remarkable range of vital transformations in both primary andsecondary metabolism. Many of these reactions demand control over reactivity ofsmall molecules that are in some cases highly energetic and prone to followingdiverse reaction pathways. In this seminar, I will examine the molecularstrategies by which two metalloenzymes harness small molecules for metabolism.Cytochrome (cyt) P460 is a cross-linked heme enzyme found in all ammonia-oxidizingbacteria (AOB). Although it is known to oxidize the highly energetic andpotently nucleophilic metabolite hydroxylamine, its physiological function hasremained elusive. I will present evidence that cyt P460 catalyzesS-nitrosylation by activating nitric oxide for nucleophilic attack by a thiol.This reaction generates one electron for respiration and subsequent hydrolysisof the S-nitrosothiol yields nitrite, thus providing an answer to thelong-standing question about how AOB complete their primary metabolic cycle.Small-molecule transformations are also central to secondary metabolism, wherethey can be incorporated into complex biosynthetic products. An unusual exampleis the O-insertion catalyzed by the radical S-adenosylmethionine enzyme DarE.Although iron-sulfur clusters are typically oxygen-sensitive, DarE employsmolecular oxygen as a substrate to form an ether cross-link during thebiosynthesis of the peptide natural product darobactin. I will discuss thedetailed characterization of key radical intermediates using advanced electronparamagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy, revealing how DarE controls radicalreactivity to achieve O-atom incorporation. Together, these studies highlightdistinct strategies by which metalloenzymes harness small molecules and controlreactive intermediates to enable challenging transformations in metabolism andnatural product biosynthesis.

events.title: Special Exhibition | Ancient Abstractions: Roman Visual Trends Beyond Naturalism
events.summary: The lifelike naturalistic bodies of Greek and Roman sculpture have been a source of wonder since the Renaissance. Indeed, the Italian Renaissance artist Vasari identified the ancient world as the time “when sculpture rose to its greatest height.” But close likenesses of the natural world are not the only visual products of the ancient past. This exhibition traces alternative visual trends in the ancient Roman world that today would be considered examples of abstraction. It focuses on monuments and motifs long pushed to the margins of our accounts of ancient art. Oversize arrangements of interlocking shapes pulsate in bold block colors from tombs, temples, and homes; stylized animals flicker into view, only to collapse once more into bright geometric arrangements; and artists adopt experimental shorthands for the depiction of space across media. Anticipating recent interests in color and form, the visual trends of antiquity emerge as far more varied than has long been told. *Ancient Abstractions is on view from November 5, 2026, through February 28, 2027, during regular museum hours (Tuesday–Friday, 10:00 AM–4:00 PM, and Saturday–Sunday, 11:00 AM–4:00 PM; closed Mondays and university holidays.*

events.title: Comics Beyond Sight
events.summary: This exhibit covers a variety of creative approaches to comics visual accessibility, and by extension visual accessibility broadly. Those approaches range from multimedia (audio and textual descriptions) through multidimensional and emerging technologies strategies (3D printing, haptics, and screen-based mobile touch interfaces). It demonstrates that comics can be made accessible. Learn about the international efforts of innovators in the realm of comics accessibility for those who are blind or have low vision, assembled by the Accessible Comics Collective at San Francisco State University (SFSU) with the expertise of blind access professionals. Emily Beitiks was the accessibility lead for the content creation of the exhibit. She is the co-director for the San Francisco Disability Cultural Center (the first civically funded disability culture center on the planet!), and prior to that, the director of the Longmore Institute on Disability. Nick Sousanis (SFSU), the lead creative organizer of the exhibit, is a Detroit native and was the first person to draw his dissertation in comics format, subsequently published as the graphic novel Unflattening. View the exhibit anytime the Hatcher Library is open, and join us for an opening presentation on Friday, October 2nd, 1:00pm - 4:00pm.

events.title: WCEE Exhibition. The Art of Memory, Paintings by Felix Lembersky
events.summary: Felix Lembersky (1913-1970) was a painter, theater stage designer, teacher, and leader of artistic groups. He began his career within the Soviet Avant-Garde in Ukraine before studying realist painting in Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg). Throughout his life he worked across realist and modernist styles that fell outside of Soviet-mandated Socialist Realism. His Execution: Babyn Yar series (ca. 1944-52) is the earliest known artistic representation of Babyn Yar, a Holocaust massacre site in Kyiv. For political reasons, these paintings, along with his later nonconformist work, were barred from exhibition in the Soviet Union. Having witnessed two world wars, the 1917 revolution, and political terror, Lembersky reflected on these experiences with candor while imbuing his work with hope and optimism. He was drawn to vulnerable, neglected, and marginalized people: children, the elderly, ethnic minorities, and industrial workers subjected to harsh labor and dangerous conditions. Regardless of their circumstances, Lembersky portrayed his subjects with empathy, dignity, and admiration. “For my father, honesty and integrity meant more than anything else. Art was an expression of freedom, individuality, and personalized creativity, without which it ceased to be art.” — Galina Lembersky, daughter Exhibit curated by Yelena Lembersky, granddaughter of Felix Lembersky, and Geneviève Zubrzycki, WCEE Director. Works on loan from the private collection of Yelena Lembersky. Contact weisercenter@umich.edu to schedule a viewing. If there is anything we can do to make this event accessible to you, please contact us at weisercenter@umich.edu. Please be aware that advance notice is necessary as some accommodations may require more time for the university to arrange.

events.title: CMENAS 2026 Fall Colloquium Series | ‘Vernacular Sovereignty’ Without a State: Kurdish Studies, Decolonial Thought, and the Making of Online Kurdistan
events.summary: What does it mean to imagine a nation without a state? This talk draws on my broader research in Kurdish studies to examine how Kurdish political life has repeatedly been organized around forms of authority and belonging that do not depend on, or wait for, a state. Taking my recent article "The Making of Online Kurdistan," co-authored with Barış Öktem, as its empirical center, the talk asks how Kurdish Generation Z constructs national belonging through digital platforms — building a transnational field of community through hashtags, online seminars, and digitally organized movements, even as this same infrastructure exposes Kurdish youth to surveillance and repression across borders. I situate this case within a longer arc of my work on Kurdish politics and within a decolonial reading of Kurdish studies more broadly. Rather than offering a general theory of sovereignty, the talk uses the Kurdish case to think through a live and unresolved question in the study of stateless nations: what forms can political authority, legitimacy, and collective imagination take when territorial statehood is foreclosed, and what is gained and lost when that struggle moves online. Mashuq Kurt is Associate Professor of Sociology in the Department of Law and Criminology at Royal Holloway, University of London. His work sits at the intersection of Middle Eastern studies and the sociology of migration and diaspora, examining how Kurds and other marginalised communities construct political authority and belonging outside the institutions of the nation-state. He is the author of *Kurdish Hizbullah in Turkey: Islamism, Violence and the State* (Pluto Press, 2017), co-editor of the *South Atlantic Quarterly Special Issue: Decolonizing Kurdish Studies *(2024) and the *Contemporary Islam Special Issue: Islam, Critique and the Canon* (2024), and has published in journals including *Current Anthropology*, *Journal of Middle East Women's Studies*, and *Social Research: An International Quarterly*. His recent article "The Making of Online Kurdistan" (*Journal of Ethnic and Migration Studies*, 2026), co-authored with Barış Öktem, examines how Kurdish Generation Z constructs national belonging through digital platforms. He was a Marie Curie Global Fellow at the London School of Economics and Yale University, has held visiting positions at Stanford and Sciences Po CERI. A regular contributor to public and policy debates, he has organised panels and given talks at the UK Parliament, Chatham House, and RUSI, and his commentary has appeared in Foreign Policy, Le Monde, and The New Arab, among others. He is also an award-winning filmmaker: his documentary *The Seven Doors *received the Jean Rouch Award from the American Anthropological Association's Society for Visual Anthropology in 2020. Join on Zoom: https://myumi.ch/pgV2y If there is anything we can do to make this event accessible to you, please contact us. Please be aware that advance notice is necessary as some accommodations may require more time for the university to arrange. events.title: WCEE Exhibition. The Art of Memory, Paintings by Felix Lembersky
events.summary: Felix Lembersky (1913-1970) was a painter, theater stage designer, teacher, and leader of artistic groups. He began his career within the Soviet Avant-Garde in Ukraine before studying realist painting in Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg). Throughout his life he worked across realist and modernist styles that fell outside of Soviet-mandated Socialist Realism. His Execution: Babyn Yar series (ca. 1944-52) is the earliest known artistic representation of Babyn Yar, a Holocaust massacre site in Kyiv. For political reasons, these paintings, along with his later nonconformist work, were barred from exhibition in the Soviet Union. Having witnessed two world wars, the 1917 revolution, and political terror, Lembersky reflected on these experiences with candor while imbuing his work with hope and optimism. He was drawn to vulnerable, neglected, and marginalized people: children, the elderly, ethnic minorities, and industrial workers subjected to harsh labor and dangerous conditions. Regardless of their circumstances, Lembersky portrayed his subjects with empathy, dignity, and admiration. “For my father, honesty and integrity meant more than anything else. Art was an expression of freedom, individuality, and personalized creativity, without which it ceased to be art.” — Galina Lembersky, daughter Exhibit curated by Yelena Lembersky, granddaughter of Felix Lembersky, and Geneviève Zubrzycki, WCEE Director. Works on loan from the private collection of Yelena Lembersky. Contact weisercenter@umich.edu to schedule a viewing. If there is anything we can do to make this event accessible to you, please contact us at weisercenter@umich.edu. events.title: “Who Counts? A History of Voting in America”
events.summary: Changes over the course of the nineteenth century in how Americans voted, from voice vote to public ballot box to private voting booth, also saw changes in the material culture that surrounded voting. Ballots and ballot boxes, campaign pins and ribbons, blank lists and pre-printed party tickets, lanterns and banners–the creative forces of the American print industry filled the country’s cities and small towns with the ephemera of electioneering. As you look at the items in this exhibit, think about what they tell us about how Americans in the past felt about voting, and about how voting felt. How did Election Days feel when they were full of parades and music and public drinking? What was it like to vote when everyone around you knew who you voted for? And, most of all, who counted as a voter, and who did the counting? On view September 11-December 22, weekdays from 12-4 pm.
events.imageAlt: “Who Counts? A History of Voting in America”

events.title: New Jazz Underground
events.summary: Sun | Jan 10 Sets 6:30pm & 9pm | $40 Cover RESERVE TABLE About the Artist New Jazz Underground, an American trio, have been described as “an innovative and ultra creative collective striving to establish themselves as a defining voice for the genre of Jazz and beyond”. Their music signals a merging of traditional sensibilities in Jazz such as the blues, swing, and improvisation with the modern influence of hip-hop, pop, and afro-latino music. Listeners were introduced to the trio’s undeniably fresh sound through viral videos of the band performing in their living room. Hundreds of thousands viewed videos such as: “they can hate but we still swingin'”, “f**k/s**t/c**t/jazz”, “sad boy jazz”, as well as many others featuring the band’s exuberant chemistry, effortless musicality, and raw ambition in sound. Abdias Armenteros (Saxophonist/Composer, 25), Sebastian Rios (Bassist/Composer, 27), TJ Reddick (Drummer, 25) have each been lauded as some of Jazz’s most promising young artists in their own right. After meeting while students at The Juilliard School, the trio began playing in the parks of NYC during lock-down in 2020. They shortly began posting to their Youtube channel that has since grown to over 100k+ subscribers. Releases such as “MF Doom Suite”, “Harlem to Havana”, and “cook/swing/work/relax” fully demonstrate the trio’s reverence towards Jazz’s icons, yet still contend in a vision to establish their own voice in the expression of new sounds that transcend genre lines. New Jazz Underground is the 2023 DCJazzPrix™ Winner. Rios is a 2024 ASCAP Herb Alpert Young Jazz Composer Award Winner. Both Reddick (BM’ 20) and Armenteros (MM’ 22) are Juillard School Graduates. Armenteros is the youngest member of the Jazz at Lincoln Center Orchestra with Wynton Marsalis. Reddick and Rios have played as sidemen for the likes of Jon Batiste, Sullivan Fortner, Emmet Cohen, and ELEW, among many more. Rios is a long-time student of the legendary bassist, Ron Carter. The group most recently was featured on NPR Music for their song “Oney Ones One” The trio not only performs, but boast their composition and production skills across a variety of mediums. Rios was a featured composer for the 2019 “New Dances”, the first ever collaboration between the Jazz and Dance divisions at The Juilliard School. He was also commissioned by Jazz at Lincoln Center to write a Suite to be performed by the trio at the 2023 Caramoor Jazz Fest. Rios’ compositions for the collective bring forth each member’s sound in a way that transcends the sum of their individual efforts. These gestures of collective musical identity are made real through the vehicle of composition tailored to each member’s unbridled talent, inspiring skill set, and transformative emotion. Creating a new standard for Jazz presentation through their online videos, New Jazz Underground have blazed a path for young Jazz musicians in the modern music landscape. Their videos attract millions of music fans through their seemingly “clickbait” presentation. However, when audiences click they are met with an authentic musical expression steeped in both modernism and tradition that provides a soulful perspective into a deeper world of music. Listeners who wouldn’t normally enjoy Jazz are brought into the music creatively through young artists who are dedicating their lives to its legacy and promise of new creative paths. NJU has a keen interest in helping students, not much younger than themselves, to develop a deeper understanding of Jazz music and the elements surrounding the creative process. Armenteros, Rios, and Reddick each have their own student studios as well as years of experience teaching students from middle school through college in topics such as Jazz history, theory, and application. Rios developed the program, “Creative Video in Modern Music” to teach intermediate to advanced Jazz students to produce their own music, and have a better understanding of the modern media landscape. Dynamic and powerful performers, New Jazz Underground possess far-reaching talents that are re-energizing the contemporary music world from the inside out. They dedicate themselves to the music continually and serve as a burgeoning benchmark for the future of Jazz to come. RESERVE TABLE

events.title: Down in Ann Arbor Town: Pictorial Maps, Campus Traditions, and the Women Who Made Them
events.summary: Celebrate the centennial of the iconic 1926 “Down in Ann Arbor Town” map by exploring the colorful history, campus traditions, and detailed artistry that made it possible. Created by Jessie Horton Koessler (Class of 1901) to help fund the Michigan League building for women, this celebrated map provides a fascinating view into 1920s campus life and the women who shaped it. Through three distinct exhibit sections, journey from the campus history that led to the map’s creation to a broader look at early 20th-century pictorial mapmaking. While enjoying the exhibit, pick up a scavenger hunt at the Clark Library desk that will inspire you to notice whimsical details in the maps discussed. Return your scavenger hunt at the desk for a small prize, while supplies last. Join the curators — Ava Pustulka (’28) and Anna Rohl, map curator at Clark Library — for a presentation on September 24 (https://myumi.ch/X8y3r), where they will share the research that went into creating the exhibit.

events.title: WCEE Exhibition. The Art of Memory, Paintings by Felix Lembersky
events.summary: Felix Lembersky (1913-1970) was a painter, theater stage designer, teacher, and leader of artistic groups. He began his career within the Soviet Avant-Garde in Ukraine before studying realist painting in Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg). Throughout his life he worked across realist and modernist styles that fell outside of Soviet-mandated Socialist Realism. His Execution: Babyn Yar series (ca. 1944-52) is the earliest known artistic representation of Babyn Yar, a Holocaust massacre site in Kyiv. For political reasons, these paintings, along with his later nonconformist work, were barred from exhibition in the Soviet Union. Having witnessed two world wars, the 1917 revolution, and political terror, Lembersky reflected on these experiences with candor while imbuing his work with hope and optimism. He was drawn to vulnerable, neglected, and marginalized people: children, the elderly, ethnic minorities, and industrial workers subjected to harsh labor and dangerous conditions. Regardless of their circumstances, Lembersky portrayed his subjects with empathy, dignity, and admiration. “For my father, honesty and integrity meant more than anything else. Art was an expression of freedom, individuality, and personalized creativity, without which it ceased to be art.” — Galina Lembersky, daughter Exhibit curated by Yelena Lembersky, granddaughter of Felix Lembersky, and Geneviève Zubrzycki, WCEE Director. Works on loan from the private collection of Yelena Lembersky. Contact weisercenter@umich.edu to schedule a viewing. If there is anything we can do to make this event accessible to you, please contact us at weisercenter@umich.edu. Please be aware that advance notice is necessary as some accommodations may require more time for the university to arrange.

events.title: Black Birth Joy
events.summary: Black Birth Joy by Tiana Lashae documents birth as a deeply personal story of connection, courage, tenderness, and joy. The photographs and stories in the exhibit challenge mainstream narratives that reduce Black birth to statistics and only amplify Black pregnant women's anxiety and hesitancy about navigating the maternal health care system. Instead, the exhibit offers evidence of joy, reminders of possibility, and a visual legacy for generations to come. Black Birth Joy was born from Lashae's belief that more positive birth stories of BIPOC families need to be seen and heard, and her photographs invite viewers to witness the people behind them: the mothers, babies, partners, families, and birthworkers. They create space for BIPOC families to see themselves represented with dignity and to witness the full range of birth experiences. Lashae's photographs also create a tangible record that can support conversations around quality of medical care, respectful treatment, and patient rights. The exhibit empowers women to prioritize and advocate for their birth experiences while also encouraging perinatal health professionals and birthworkers to center the humanity, dignity, and individual experiences of patients and families. The exhibit comprises over 30 photographs as well as stories of mothers whose births were documented by Lashae, a doula and birth/newborn photographer whose work has been published in Everyday Birth Magazine, an international publication. The physical exhibit is accompanied by a virtual component that encourages audiences to engage with each mother's birth story. The Lane Hall Exhibit Space is sponsored by the Institute for Research on Women and Gender (IRWG) and the Department of Women’s and Gender Studies (WGS) at the University of Michigan. Black Birth Joy Thursday, October 1, 2026 – Friday, January 15, 2027 Lane Hall Exhibit Space, 204 S State St., Ann Arbor, MI Open M–F, 9AM–5PM

events.title: Jessi Grieser, carillon
events.summary: LSA faculty member Jessi Grieser performs on the Charles Baird Carillon, an instrument of 53 bronze bells located inside the Burton Memorial Tower. The largest bell, which strikes the hour, weighs 12 tons, while the smallest bell, 4½ octaves above, weighs just 15 pounds. Thirty-minute recitals are performed on the Charles Baird Carillon at noon every weekday that classes are in session, followed by visitor Q&A with the carillonist. The bell chamber may be accessed via a combination of elevator and stairs. Take the elevator to the highest floor possible (floor 8), and then climb two flights of stairs (39 steps) to the bell chamber (floor 10). Hearing protection earmuffs are provided for visitors. Be prepared to walk on ice and snow in the bell chamber during winter. Built in 1936, the Charles Baird Carillon is not ADA accessible. Visitors with mobility concerns are invited to visit the Lurie Carillon.

events.title: The Limits of Targeted Hiring Subsidies: Evidence from the Work Opportunity Tax Credit (joint with Manisha Jain and Jeffrey Weaver)
events.summary: Employer-side wage subsidies are widely used to promote employment among disadvantaged workers. We study how such subsidies translate into firm hiring behavior using the federal Work Opportunity Tax Credit, which subsidizes up to 40% of first-year wages and covers over two million hires annually. Using linked administrative data from Wisconsin and multiple quasi- experimental designs, we find consistent and precise null effects on hiring, earnings, retention, and related outcomes across designs and firm types. Original data on firm hiring practices suggest two mechanisms that can limit employer-side subsidy efficacy: perceived legal risks discourage eligibility screening and organizational frictions attenuate decision-makers’ responsiveness.

events.summary: Thurs | Jan 28 Sets at 7pm & 8:30pm | $25 Cover RESERVE TABLE About the Artist Over the period of 20 years as a professional jazz pianist and 7 full-length album appearances (3 as leader), Keigo Hirakawa has transformed himself from a student of the jazz masters to an artist with vision and unique sense of expressions. Though his engagements may include jazz clubs to music halls and jazz festivals, he takes the time to contribute to his home music scene through mentorship and appearances with up-and-coming talents. The jazz piano trio he leads is well-known throughout the Midwest for their willingness to be musically spontaneous on stage, exploring original compositions and redefining jazz standards to make it their own. Sought after for his articulate use of harmonic and rhythmic vocabulary and his leadership style on the bandstand, Hirakawa can be heard throughout the US and internationally. Trained in New York City and at the New England Conservatory of Music in Boston, Hirakawa is fortunate to have been mentored by many world-class jazz artists, including Danilo Perez, Stephen Scott, Harold Danko, Alan Pasqua, Ran Blake, Cecil McBee, Ralph Peterson, Jerry Bergonzi, Donald Byrd, John McNeil, George Garzone, Bob Moses, and Walt Weiskopf. He has appeared on stage alongside Donald Byrd, Joe Lovano, Robert Hurst, JD Allen, Carla Cook, Bobby Lavell, Bob Moses, and Allen Vizzutti; toured with Stacy Dillard, Duane Eubanks and Noah Preminger; has performed with the Springfield Symphony Orchestra; and his latest album features the jazz bass legend Robert Hurst. He was the acting director of the Cornell University Jazz Ensembles in 2000-2001, during which time he welcomed Donald Byrd, Jimmy Heath, Wycliffe Gordon, Terell Stafford, Vincent Herring, and Joe Chambers onto the stage as guest soloists. events.title: Special Exhibition | Ancient Abstractions: Roman Visual Trends Beyond Naturalism
events.summary: The lifelike naturalistic bodies of Greek and Roman sculpture have been a source of wonder since the Renaissance. Indeed, the Italian Renaissance artist Vasari identified the ancient world as the time “when sculpture rose to its greatest height.” But close likenesses of the natural world are not the only visual products of the ancient past. This exhibition traces alternative visual trends in the ancient Roman world that today would be considered examples of abstraction. It focuses on monuments and motifs long pushed to the margins of our accounts of ancient art. Oversize arrangements of interlocking shapes pulsate in bold block colors from tombs, temples, and homes; stylized animals flicker into view, only to collapse once more into bright geometric arrangements; and artists adopt experimental shorthands for the depiction of space across media. Anticipating recent interests in color and form, the visual trends of antiquity emerge as far more varied than has long been told. *Ancient Abstractions is on view from November 5, 2026, through February 28, 2027, during regular museum hours (Tuesday–Friday, 10:00 AM–4:00 PM, and Saturday–Sunday, 11:00 AM–4:00 PM; closed Mondays and university holidays.*

events.title: Borrowing Strength in Multiple Testing with Compound p-values
events.summary: Many large-scale multiple testing problems in high-throughput biology involve thousands of units (e.g., genes or proteins) but only a small number of replicates per unit. A key observation in the microarray literature around the turn of the century was that standard t-tests may be nearly powerless in this setting. This motivated the development of methods such as the B-statistic (Lönnstedt and Speed, 2002), Significance Analysis of Microarrays (SAM; Tusher, Tibshirani and Chu, 2001), and limma (Smyth, 2004), which borrow information across units. We study this type of borrowing across units through the lens of compound p-values. Unlike bona fide p-values, compound p-values need not be valid for each hypothesis separately, but instead satisfy an average superuniformity property across the null hypotheses. We first explain how compound p-values arise both from a nonparametric version of limma and from SAM. We then use the compound p-value perspective to construct a procedure that achieves the asymptotic power of the oracle Bayes rule in a sparse regime under the hierarchical model underlying the B-statistic and provides finite-sample frequentist control of the false discovery rate without requiring this hierarchical model to hold.
events.imageAlt: Borrowing Strength in Multiple Testing with Compound p-values

events.title: AI Futures Keynote: Isabelle Hau
events.summary: The Industrial Revolution elevated IQ, the cognitive abilities needed for an economy built around knowledge and analytical skill. The late 20th century expanded our understanding through EQ, recognizing the importance of understanding ourselves and others. Now, the AI revolution calls for another evolution in human intelligence: Relational Intelligence (RQ), our capacity to build trust, make meaning together, connect across differences, collaborate, navigate conflict, and repair. Universities have a critical role in this transition. As they prepare students for an AI-shaped future, they must revisit not only what we teach and how we learn, but how we relate, developing AI fluency alongside the deeply human capacities that will matter even more in an age of intelligent machines. This session asks a defining question: If AI changes what it means to be intelligent, how should education evolve what we teach, what we measure, and what we value? *About AI Futures Keynote Speaker Series* The Center for Academic Innovation is convening leading voices in academia to examine emerging applications of artificial intelligence in higher education. The AI Futures keynote speaker series is a critical examination of how artificial intelligence is reshaping teaching and learning as we consider the future of life changing education at Michigan

Essayistic and reflexive, “Hard to Swallow” recounts Wey’s explosive career while building a critique of the social structures that disenfranchise Black peoples globally. Through episodes that follow Wey from New Orleans’ food scene to Detroit’s mayor’s office to the show’s contentious debut in Cannes, “Hard to Swallow” is unlike any food show on air right now. Following the screening, prominent Detroit-based chef Ederique “Chef E” Goudia will moderate a discussion with show creators Wey and Schear.

events.title: Black Birth Joy
events.summary: Black Birth Joy by Tiana Lashae documents birth as a deeply personal story of connection, courage, tenderness, and joy. The photographs and stories in the exhibit challenge mainstream narratives that reduce Black birth to statistics and only amplify Black pregnant women's anxiety and hesitancy about navigating the maternal health care system. Instead, the exhibit offers evidence of joy, reminders of possibility, and a visual legacy for generations to come. Black Birth Joy was born from Lashae's belief that more positive birth stories of BIPOC families need to be seen and heard, and her photographs invite viewers to witness the people behind them: the mothers, babies, partners, families, and birthworkers. They create space for BIPOC families to see themselves represented with dignity and to witness the full range of birth experiences. Lashae's photographs also create a tangible record that can support conversations around quality of medical care, respectful treatment, and patient rights. The exhibit empowers women to prioritize and advocate for their birth experiences while also encouraging perinatal health professionals and birthworkers to center the humanity, dignity, and individual experiences of patients and families. The exhibit comprises over 30 photographs as well as stories of mothers whose births were documented by Lashae, a doula and birth/newborn photographer whose work has been published in Everyday Birth Magazine, an international publication. The physical exhibit is accompanied by a virtual component that encourages audiences to engage with each mother's birth story. The Lane Hall Exhibit Space is sponsored by the Institute for Research on Women and Gender (IRWG) and the Department of Women’s and Gender Studies (WGS) at the University of Michigan. Black Birth Joy Thursday, October 1, 2026 – Friday, January 15, 2027 Lane Hall Exhibit Space, 204 S State St., Ann Arbor, MI Open M–F, 9AM–5PM

events.title: Down in Ann Arbor Town: Pictorial Maps, Campus Traditions, and the Women Who Made Them
events.summary: Celebrate the centennial of the iconic 1926 “Down in Ann Arbor Town” map by exploring the colorful history, campus traditions, and detailed artistry that made it possible. Created by Jessie Horton Koessler (Class of 1901) to help fund the Michigan League building for women, this celebrated map provides a fascinating view into 1920s campus life and the women who shaped it. Through three distinct exhibit sections, journey from the campus history that led to the map’s creation to a broader look at early 20th-century pictorial mapmaking. While enjoying the exhibit, pick up a scavenger hunt at the Clark Library desk that will inspire you to notice whimsical details in the maps discussed. Return your scavenger hunt at the desk for a small prize, while supplies last. Join the curators — Ava Pustulka (’28) and Anna Rohl, map curator at Clark Library — for a presentation on September 24 (https://myumi.ch/X8y3r), where they will share the research that went into creating the exhibit.

events.title: Faster and More Fun: American Home Cooking in the 1920s
events.summary: Visit the Hatcher Gallery Exhibit Room to see historical materials that illustrate women’s changing relationship with food, cooking, and technology during the heady decade of the 1920s, sandwiched between WWI and the Great Depression. This exhibit features materials from the Janice Bluestein Longone Culinary Archive, as well as select items from the Art, Architecture, and Engineering Special Collections and the Transportation History Collection. As America rang in a new decade in the 1920s, cookbook authors and appliance manufacturers stood ready to offer the newly emancipated and forward-thinking American woman a vision for her future, a vision that would be scientifically grounded, speedy enough to make time for leisure as well as housework, and guaranteed to bring fun to that most humdrum of chores: planning and preparing meals for a family three times a day, 365 days a year.

events.title: WCEE Exhibition. The Art of Memory, Paintings by Felix Lembersky
events.summary: Felix Lembersky (1913-1970) was a painter, theater stage designer, teacher, and leader of artistic groups. He began his career within the Soviet Avant-Garde in Ukraine before studying realist painting in Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg). Throughout his life he worked across realist and modernist styles that fell outside of Soviet-mandated Socialist Realism. His Execution: Babyn Yar series (ca. 1944-52) is the earliest known artistic representation of Babyn Yar, a Holocaust massacre site in Kyiv. For political reasons, these paintings, along with his later nonconformist work, were barred from exhibition in the Soviet Union. Having witnessed two world wars, the 1917 revolution, and political terror, Lembersky reflected on these experiences with candor while imbuing his work with hope and optimism. He was drawn to vulnerable, neglected, and marginalized people: children, the elderly, ethnic minorities, and industrial workers subjected to harsh labor and dangerous conditions. Regardless of their circumstances, Lembersky portrayed his subjects with empathy, dignity, and admiration. “For my father, honesty and integrity meant more than anything else. Art was an expression of freedom, individuality, and personalized creativity, without which it ceased to be art.” — Galina Lembersky, daughter Exhibit curated by Yelena Lembersky, granddaughter of Felix Lembersky, and Geneviève Zubrzycki, WCEE Director. Works on loan from the private collection of Yelena Lembersky. Contact weisercenter@umich.edu to schedule a viewing. If there is anything we can do to make this event accessible to you, please contact us at weisercenter@umich.edu. Please be aware that advance notice is necessary as some accommodations may require more time for the university to arrange.

events.title: Down in Ann Arbor Town: Pictorial Maps, Campus Traditions, and the Women Who Made Them
events.summary: Celebrate the centennial of the iconic 1926 “Down in Ann Arbor Town” map by exploring the colorful history, campus traditions, and detailed artistry that made it possible. Created by Jessie Horton Koessler (Class of 1901) to help fund the Michigan League building for women, this celebrated map provides a fascinating view into 1920s campus life and the women who shaped it. Through three distinct exhibit sections, journey from the campus history that led to the map’s creation to a broader look at early 20th-century pictorial mapmaking. While enjoying the exhibit, pick up a scavenger hunt at the Clark Library desk that will inspire you to notice whimsical details in the maps discussed. Return your scavenger hunt at the desk for a small prize, while supplies last. Join the curators — Ava Pustulka (’28) and Anna Rohl, map curator at Clark Library — for a presentation on September 24 (https://myumi.ch/X8y3r), where they will share the research that went into creating the exhibit.

In addition to her albums, Olivia has released standout singles including “Close To You,” “Human Nature,” and “Mercy, Mercy, Mercy,” reimagining beloved classics through a contemporary jazz lens. Olivia performs in settings ranging from intimate duos to full big band collaborations and appears regularly throughout Michigan and neighboring states. She returned as a featured guest vocalist with the Ann Arbor Symphony Orchestra for consecutive Holiday Pops seasons in 2024 and 2025. She has been honored with the Preservation of Jazz Excellence Award for Best Vocalist and has received multiple nominations from the Detroit Music Awards. A frequent collaborator with pianist Scott Gwinnell, bassist Paul Keller, and JUNO Award-winning vocalist Caity Gyorgy, Olivia continues to shape her artistic voice through performance, composition, and production-contributing to the evolving landscape of contemporary jazz. events.title: Special Exhibition | Ancient Abstractions: Roman Visual Trends Beyond Naturalism
events.summary: The lifelike naturalistic bodies of Greek and Roman sculpture have been a source of wonder since the Renaissance. Indeed, the Italian Renaissance artist Vasari identified the ancient world as the time “when sculpture rose to its greatest height.” But close likenesses of the natural world are not the only visual products of the ancient past. This exhibition traces alternative visual trends in the ancient Roman world that today would be considered examples of abstraction. It focuses on monuments and motifs long pushed to the margins of our accounts of ancient art. Oversize arrangements of interlocking shapes pulsate in bold block colors from tombs, temples, and homes; stylized animals flicker into view, only to collapse once more into bright geometric arrangements; and artists adopt experimental shorthands for the depiction of space across media. Anticipating recent interests in color and form, the visual trends of antiquity emerge as far more varied than has long been told. *Ancient Abstractions is on view from November 5, 2026, through February 28, 2027, during regular museum hours (Tuesday–Friday, 10:00 AM–4:00 PM, and Saturday–Sunday, 11:00 AM–4:00 PM; closed Mondays and university holidays.*

events.title: Special Exhibition | Ancient Abstractions: Roman Visual Trends Beyond Naturalism
events.summary: The lifelike naturalistic bodies of Greek and Roman sculpture have been a source of wonder since the Renaissance. Indeed, the Italian Renaissance artist Vasari identified the ancient world as the time “when sculpture rose to its greatest height.” But close likenesses of the natural world are not the only visual products of the ancient past. This exhibition traces alternative visual trends in the ancient Roman world that today would be considered examples of abstraction. It focuses on monuments and motifs long pushed to the margins of our accounts of ancient art. Oversize arrangements of interlocking shapes pulsate in bold block colors from tombs, temples, and homes; stylized animals flicker into view, only to collapse once more into bright geometric arrangements; and artists adopt experimental shorthands for the depiction of space across media. Anticipating recent interests in color and form, the visual trends of antiquity emerge as far more varied than has long been told. *Ancient Abstractions is on view from November 5, 2026, through February 28, 2027, during regular museum hours (Tuesday–Friday, 10:00 AM–4:00 PM, and Saturday–Sunday, 11:00 AM–4:00 PM; closed Mondays and university holidays.*

events.title: RCGD Fall Seminar Series: Global Perspectives on Culture and Health (Beverly Strassmann)
events.summary: RCGD Fall 2026 Seminar Series: Global Perspectives on Culture & Health, meets Mondays 3:30 to 5 at ISR Thompson 6050. Global Perspectives on Culture and Health explores fundamental aspects of human life. Culture facilitates human interaction by providing meaning to lived experience. Accounting for culture in both theories and methods potentially advances the study of health by connecting the macro and micro levels of human experience. Yet, culture should be understood as dynamic and complex. It fundamentally shapes individuals and simultaneously is shaped by individuals. The importance of systematically attending to culture includes topics of values, language, immigration, and society. Theories and methods that incorporate culture hold great potential for advancing the understanding of health outcomes and health trajectories in various global contexts. The speakers for this series will focus on various aspects of culture and diverse groups living in the U.S. and across the globe to address the ways in which attending to culture helps clarify and overcome challenges to good health. The Group Dynamics Seminar series is considered one of the longest running seminar series in the social sciences. It has been running uninterruptedly since it was founded by Kurt Lewin in the 1920’s in Berlin. The seminar series runs every semester on a theme chosen by faculty organizer/s who are affiliated with the Research Center for Group Dynamics at the Institute for Social Research. A very important feature of this seminar today is its interdisciplinary nature. Recent themes have included political polarization, evolution and human behavior, and cultural psychology. In person: ISR Thompson 1430, unless otherwise specified. Organized by Kristine Ajrouch and Sela Panapasa Events are not recorded, but as permissions allow, interviews with speakers are later posted to our YouTube playlist.

events.title: WCEE Exhibition. The Art of Memory, Paintings by Felix Lembersky
events.summary: Felix Lembersky (1913-1970) was a painter, theater stage designer, teacher, and leader of artistic groups. He began his career within the Soviet Avant-Garde in Ukraine before studying realist painting in Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg). Throughout his life he worked across realist and modernist styles that fell outside of Soviet-mandated Socialist Realism. His Execution: Babyn Yar series (ca. 1944-52) is the earliest known artistic representation of Babyn Yar, a Holocaust massacre site in Kyiv. For political reasons, these paintings, along with his later nonconformist work, were barred from exhibition in the Soviet Union. Having witnessed two world wars, the 1917 revolution, and political terror, Lembersky reflected on these experiences with candor while imbuing his work with hope and optimism. He was drawn to vulnerable, neglected, and marginalized people: children, the elderly, ethnic minorities, and industrial workers subjected to harsh labor and dangerous conditions. Regardless of their circumstances, Lembersky portrayed his subjects with empathy, dignity, and admiration. “For my father, honesty and integrity meant more than anything else. Art was an expression of freedom, individuality, and personalized creativity, without which it ceased to be art.” — Galina Lembersky, daughter Exhibit curated by Yelena Lembersky, granddaughter of Felix Lembersky, and Geneviève Zubrzycki, WCEE Director. Works on loan from the private collection of Yelena Lembersky. Contact weisercenter@umich.edu to schedule a viewing. If there is anything we can do to make this event accessible to you, please contact us at weisercenter@umich.edu. Please be aware that advance notice is necessary as some accommodations may require more time for the university to arrange.

About Memory Cafés: - Memory Cafés are community-based gatherings that provide safe, inclusive environments for people experiencing dementia or other cognitive changes, along with their care partners. - Through storytelling, music, movement, visual art, and more, these spaces foster joy, reduce stigma, and help people feel seen and supported. - They do not require a medical diagnosis to attend. About Legato Memory Café: - It is a safe and welcoming space where we value creative expression, building community, and supporting each other. - Activities are designed to make people of all abilities feel comfortable and engaged. - Socializing and creative exploration take center stage. - You’ll find great conversation, icebreakers, refreshments, and engaging activities/crafts. - Complimentary parking. What to Expect: - Upon arrival, you will get a name tag and have a few minutes to settle in before we begin the activity. - We will do an activity or craft—all levels/abilities welcome! events.title: Special Exhibition | Ancient Abstractions: Roman Visual Trends Beyond Naturalism
events.summary: The lifelike naturalistic bodies of Greek and Roman sculpture have been a source of wonder since the Renaissance. Indeed, the Italian Renaissance artist Vasari identified the ancient world as the time “when sculpture rose to its greatest height.” But close likenesses of the natural world are not the only visual products of the ancient past. This exhibition traces alternative visual trends in the ancient Roman world that today would be considered examples of abstraction. It focuses on monuments and motifs long pushed to the margins of our accounts of ancient art. Oversize arrangements of interlocking shapes pulsate in bold block colors from tombs, temples, and homes; stylized animals flicker into view, only to collapse once more into bright geometric arrangements; and artists adopt experimental shorthands for the depiction of space across media. Anticipating recent interests in color and form, the visual trends of antiquity emerge as far more varied than has long been told. *Ancient Abstractions is on view from November 5, 2026, through February 28, 2027, during regular museum hours (Tuesday–Friday, 10:00 AM–4:00 PM, and Saturday–Sunday, 11:00 AM–4:00 PM; closed Mondays and university holidays.*

events.title: Between Slavery and Incarceration
events.summary: This talk aims to make sense of some puzzling patterns in the incarceration rates of Black and White Americans since slavery, particularly why the Black incarceration rate was lower in the South than in the North for much of the 20th century, why it was lowest in the South’s cotton belt, and why it began to increase in the second half of the 20th century. I argue that these patterns partially reflect the long history of the demand for agricultural labor in the South. To evaluate this claim, I examine how two shocks to agricultural labor demand—the boll weevil infestation and the introduction of the mechanical cotton harvester—affected incarceration in the South. The talk will close with some reflections on how these findings clarify the relationship between incarceration and slavery, the criminal surety system, and broader shifts in the agricultural economy in the United States.

events.title: Like the flowing river
events.summary: Artist Tomoyuki Ueno creates individual works and installations where nature appears to be in an endless conversation with form, one echoing the other, a repetition. They are a combination of certainty and ephemerality, as if hinged between living and loss. The specificity of Ueno’s sculptural works reads like poetry. Ueno’s installation offers visitors time away, for contemplation, to draw inward, to come inside, to ask the question, “How are art and the everyday intertwined?” Honoring the Buddhist philosophy of impermanence, one becomes a continuation of the other. The artist intends the space to offer a restorative and meditative experience. This exhibition includes artworks created from natural materials foraged by the artist while in artist residency in Ann Arbor. *The title refers to the opening line of Hōjōki, written by 13th-century Japanese Buddhist monk Kamo no Chōmei: "The flow of the river is ceaseless, and the water is never the same…"*

events.title: Incorporations: Capitalism and Collective Life with Associate Professor Matthew Hull
events.summary: Join the U-M Department of Anthropology for the annual Roy A. Rappaport Lecture Series! Associate Professor Matthew Hull will present the fall 2026 series, titled “Incorporations: Capitalism and Collective Life.” Abstract: “Corporations are often seen as purely economic actors, but they have been central to Anglo-American governance for centuries—pioneers of democratic assembly, speech, citizenship, and constitutions. Many features of corporations, once grounded in democratic ideals, now foster the unresponsiveness of these institutions. These lectures will include discussion of a diverse array of corporations: medieval guilds, the English East India Company, Alaska Native corporations, and caste-based corporations in India.” Rappaport lectures will take place on the following fall Fridays from 3 to 4:30 p.m. in West Hall Room 411. They are free and open to the public: Friday, Sept. 25 “Corporate Persons in Human Law: Reproduction, Kinship, Jurisdiction” Friday, Oct. 23 “Freedom and Citizenship: Corporate Membership and the Making of Exclusion” Friday, Nov. 13 “Meetings and Speech: Corporate Mediations of Will” Friday, Dec. 4 “Sharing and Inequality in Corporations” VIRTUAL PARTICIPATION LINK: https://umich.zoom.us/j/91475190155 REGISTRATION IS APPRECIATED for planning purposes: https://myumi.ch/e77Ax If you need accommodations to attend, please email anthro.exec.secretary@umich.edu. ABOUT ASSOCIATE PROFESSOR MATTHEW HULL Matthew Hull is Associate Professor of Anthropology at the University of Michigan. His research focuses on the nexus of signification, technology, and institutions. His book, “Government of Paper: The Materiality of Bureaucracy in Urban Pakistan,” winner of the 2019 J.I. Staley Prize from the School of Advanced Research, examines governance as a semiotic and material practice. He has worked on urban planning in 1960s India and police communication systems and lotteries in contemporary India. He is currently writing a book on how early modern corporations shaped democratic governance and continue to structure contemporary political life.

events.title: WCEE Exhibition. The Art of Memory, Paintings by Felix Lembersky
events.summary: Felix Lembersky (1913-1970) was a painter, theater stage designer, teacher, and leader of artistic groups. He began his career within the Soviet Avant-Garde in Ukraine before studying realist painting in Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg). Throughout his life he worked across realist and modernist styles that fell outside of Soviet-mandated Socialist Realism. His Execution: Babyn Yar series (ca. 1944-52) is the earliest known artistic representation of Babyn Yar, a Holocaust massacre site in Kyiv. For political reasons, these paintings, along with his later nonconformist work, were barred from exhibition in the Soviet Union. Having witnessed two world wars, the 1917 revolution, and political terror, Lembersky reflected on these experiences with candor while imbuing his work with hope and optimism. He was drawn to vulnerable, neglected, and marginalized people: children, the elderly, ethnic minorities, and industrial workers subjected to harsh labor and dangerous conditions. Regardless of their circumstances, Lembersky portrayed his subjects with empathy, dignity, and admiration. “For my father, honesty and integrity meant more than anything else. Art was an expression of freedom, individuality, and personalized creativity, without which it ceased to be art.” — Galina Lembersky, daughter Exhibit curated by Yelena Lembersky, granddaughter of Felix Lembersky, and Geneviève Zubrzycki, WCEE Director. Works on loan from the private collection of Yelena Lembersky. Contact weisercenter@umich.edu to schedule a viewing. If there is anything we can do to make this event accessible to you, please contact us at weisercenter@umich.edu. Please be aware that advance notice is necessary as some accommodations may require more time for the university to arrange.

events.title: Antje Duvekot & David Berkeley
events.summary: Ticket prices on our website reflect all-in pricing for purchases made online or by phone. This means the price you see includes the ticket price plus MUTO’s ticket processing fee. Tickets may be purchased with no included fees in person at The Ark during box office hours. Originally born in Germany and transplanted to the U.S. as a young teen, Antje Duvekot began honing her observational skills through a lens of biculturalism when she picked up a guitar in high school. Some years later, the confessional folk of Dar Williams and Ani DiFranco gave her license to share those observations, no matter how personal, in her first emerging songs. She has never let go of the tenet of vulnerability, building a celebrated career around songs that transform deeply personal experiences into something universal. Santa Fe-based songwriter and author David Berkeley writes songs capable of both breaking and mending the heart. A standout guest on This American Life, he’s won many songwriting awards and honors including ASCAPs Johnny Mercer Songwriting Award. Berkeley has released 9 studio albums, a live album, and authored 2 books. Berkeley’s newest album, A Pail Full of Fire, is a masterclass on songwriting and singing. Like all of Berkeley’s catalogue, the music begs you to lean in and listen close, as each song speaks to what matters in this life.

events.title: CREES Noon Lecture. Who Defines Central Asia? Decolonial Disruptions from Below
events.summary: A consequential shift is taking place in Central Asian studies today. What started as a slow rejection of the idea that the region benefited from Soviet control has turned into a decentralized, collective effort to revise the region’s relationship to its colonial identity and to search for indigenous interpretations of the self. A recent Cambridge Element publication co-authored by Erica Marat and Aizada Arystanbek explores the current decolonial disruptions in Central Asia – how the region is being redefined by its inhabitants, both in discourse and in practice. It captures the main areas of activism in memory studies, language activism, art installations, and transnational solidarity networks. Decolonial discussions are gaining traction, challenging political elites’ hegemony over national identity formation. Such changes harbor the potential to profoundly alter Russia’s influence in the areas it once controlled. Decolonial disruptions are reshaping how Central Asians think about their past and imagine their future. Dr. Erica Marat is an adjunct professor at the Center for Security Studies, Georgetown University. Her research focuses on violence, mobilization and security institutions in Europe, Central Asia, India, and Mexico. She is an author of several books, including "Decolonial Disruptions in Central Asia: Discussion, Practices, and Networks" (Cambridge Elements 2026) and "Transformative Violence: When Routine Cruelty Sparks Historic Mobilization" (Oxford University Press 2024). Her articles have appeared in "Foreign Affairs," "Foreign Policy," "Just Security," and "Open Democracy." If there is anything we can do to make this event accessible to you, please contact us at crees@umich.edu. Please be aware that advance notice is necessary as some accommodations may require more time for the university to arrange. *Part of the International Institute Theme Year: Sovereignty* https://myumi.ch/ii-theme

events.title: Special Exhibition | Ancient Abstractions: Roman Visual Trends Beyond Naturalism
events.summary: The lifelike naturalistic bodies of Greek and Roman sculpture have been a source of wonder since the Renaissance. Indeed, the Italian Renaissance artist Vasari identified the ancient world as the time “when sculpture rose to its greatest height.” But close likenesses of the natural world are not the only visual products of the ancient past. This exhibition traces alternative visual trends in the ancient Roman world that today would be considered examples of abstraction. It focuses on monuments and motifs long pushed to the margins of our accounts of ancient art. Oversize arrangements of interlocking shapes pulsate in bold block colors from tombs, temples, and homes; stylized animals flicker into view, only to collapse once more into bright geometric arrangements; and artists adopt experimental shorthands for the depiction of space across media. Anticipating recent interests in color and form, the visual trends of antiquity emerge as far more varied than has long been told. *Ancient Abstractions is on view from November 5, 2026, through February 28, 2027, during regular museum hours (Tuesday–Friday, 10:00 AM–4:00 PM, and Saturday–Sunday, 11:00 AM–4:00 PM; closed Mondays and university holidays.*

Trained in the Radif tradition and immersed in modern santoor techniques, Babak Soleimani weaves jazz and electronic textures into his instrumentals on two exploratory EPs: Dhow and Farewell Pond. Developed by the Judy and Stanley Frankel Detroit Observatory and featuring the work of its student docents, “Fill the Ranks” includes historic artifacts, digital animations, and interactive elements spanning two floors.
